author: DPA
title: New York Times challenges subpoenas of its journalists - NewsBreak
text:
36 minutes ago
FILE PHOTO - US President Donald Trump boards Air Force One at Gimhae International Airport in Busan. (is associated with: «New York Times challenges subpoenas of its journalists») Daniel Torok/White House/dpa The New York Times on Wednesday began legal action to challenge subpoenas to journalists after they reported on possible security concerns linked to President Donald Trump's new official aircraft.
The New York Times asked a federal judge to quash the subpoenas, which were delivered in some cases by federal officials to journalists' homes on Friday in what was seen as an attempt to intimidate independent media.
The Times' lead newsroom lawyer David McCraw said the subpoenas were "abusive" and "improper" and should be quashed by a court.
"As we set out in our motion, these subpoenas are brought in bad faith to punish The Times for its coverage," McCraw said in a statement. "They violate the constitutional rights of The Times and its journalists."
The subpoenas had ordered three journalists to appear before a grand jury and disclose their confidential sources.
Citing anonymous sources, the journalists had reported that Trump flew from the NATO summit in Turkey to the British air base at Mildenhall on the old Air Force One on the advice of the Secret Service. There he transferred to the new aircraft, which was a gift from Qatar.
In a separate report, the newspaper wrote that the new jet did not yet have all the security and defence systems of the old presidential aircraft.
However, the government and Trump denied that security concerns were the reason for the change of aircraft. Trump stated on several occasions that the stopover served to show the new aircraft to military personnel.
Since the start of his second term, Trump's administration has been cracking down on US media outlets.
Earlier this year, the Department of Justice attempted to compel journalists from the Wall Street Journal and the Washington Post to provide evidence in investigations into whistleblowing.
These subpoenas were later withdrawn following legal challenges by the media organizations.
